comparison: Perfect agreement. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support claims C1 and C129 regarding HMMR identification as an abundant MAP in neurons through proteomics. Peer reviewers accept this as the starting point without challenge, while OpenEval notes the methodology is appropriate though raw data is not provided.

Strong agreement. Both support loss-of-function findings (C12-C14, C23-C26, C33) showing HMMR depletion reduces neurite length and branching. Peer reviewers also explicitly affirm summary claims C75 and C78 about HMMR's necessity for neuronal morphology, which OpenEval addresses separately in R23.

Perfect agreement. Both support gain-of-function findings (C15, C29-C32, C76-C77) showing HMMR overexpression increases neurite length and branching. Both acknowledge the complementary nature of bidirectional loss- and gain-of-function experiments strengthens conclusions.

Strong agreement. Both support rescue experiments (C27-C28) demonstrating human HMMR complements mouse HMMR function. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of well-controlled experimental design, while OpenEval explicitly notes it validates specificity and rules out off-target effects.

Strong agreement. Both support HMMR localization as puncta on microtubules (C16-C17, C35-C36, C79-C80, C132). OpenEval emphasizes antibody validation controls (C34), while peer reviewers accept the overall localization findings including both immunofluorescence and PLA data without challenge.

Strong agreement. Both support PLA data (C39-C43) demonstrating HMMR-microtubule association. OpenEval emphasizes the appropriateness of PLA technique and negative controls, while peer reviewers accept PLA as part of well-controlled localization experiments. Peer R6 also includes antibody validation (C34) that OpenEval addresses in R12.

Strong agreement. Both support acetylated tubulin findings (C18, C48-C50) showing bidirectional effects of HMMR on microtubule stability. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and complementary experimental design, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm these findings as evidence for HMMR's role in regulating microtubule stability. Peer R9 also includes nocodazole data (C55).

Strong agreement. Both support nocodazole resistance experiments (C51-C54) as evidence for HMMR's microtubule-stabilizing function. OpenEval emphasizes dose-response design and consistency with acetylated tubulin data, while peer reviewers accept this as demonstrating HMMR regulates stability. Peer R10 also includes interpretation C91 that OpenEval addresses separately in R18.

Strong agreement. Both support EB3 live-cell imaging findings (C56-C63) showing HMMR affects microtubule dynamics. OpenEval notes C57-C58 describe only trends without statistical significance, while peer reviewers affirm the overall impact on dynamics. Peer R11 also includes claim C19 not in OpenEval R8.

Strong agreement. Both support PLA findings (C20, C67-C69, C71-C72, C74, C81, C95) showing HMMR affects TPX2-microtubule interaction. OpenEval emphasizes bidirectional effects and mechanistic explanation, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm HMMR promotes TPX2 function and microtubule nucleation. Both accept this as a key mechanistic finding.

Strong agreement. Both support observations of looped microtubules with HMMR overexpression (C37-C38, C93). OpenEval connects this to microtubule-bundling activity and axon branching via literature, while peer reviewers explicitly note looped microtubules as indicative of increased stability. Peer R7 does not include C92 that OpenEval addresses.

Strong agreement. Both support antibody validation (C34) showing reduced HMMR signal in knockdown neurons. OpenEval treats this as a separate essential control for immunofluorescence interpretation, while peer reviewers implicitly accept it as part of the well-controlled localization experiments that include both antibody validation and PLA data.

Perfect agreement. Both support colocalization analysis (C44-C46) showing HMMR puncta do not represent microtubule plus-ends. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative Pearson correlation and adequate sample size, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of HMMR characterization consistent with its function along microtubule shafts.

Strong agreement. Both support the novelty and significance of findings (C82, C133). OpenEval notes this is the most comprehensive mechanistic characterization though questions if 'first time' claim is overstated, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm novelty as 'first step in deciphering' mitotic MAP influence in neurons and adding 'novel insight' into MAP-mediated regulation.

OpenEval supports claims C21-C22 about hippocampal neuron culture methodology based on established reference (Banker and Goslin, 1998), noting it's appropriate for reducing variability though neuronal composition not independently verified. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports background/literature claims C2-C11 and C83-C90 about HMMR's known roles in mitosis and other systems, presented as established knowledge with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focus on novel experimental findings rather than background claims.

OpenEval supports literature claims C64-C66 and C96-C98 about HMMR-TPX2 interaction and regulation, providing mechanistic context for current PLA results. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers accept the mechanistic interpretation without separately evaluating background literature.

Divergent evaluation types. OpenEval rates speculative claims C99 and C104 as UNCERTAIN, noting they are hypotheses requiring experimental testing though reasonably presented. Peer reviewers support the mechanistic discussion including C104 about branching regulation, accepting it as part of the overall interpretation. Only C104 overlaps between evaluations.

Divergent evaluation types. OpenEval rates C91 (stability as 'main mechanism') as UNCERTAIN, noting it's an interpretation rather than demonstrated mechanism with relative importance not quantified. Peer reviewers support this interpretation, accepting that nocodazole resistance and stability data argue HMMR regulates stability driving outgrowth.

OpenEval supports literature claims C100-C103 about microtubule nucleation and neuronal branching relationships, providing context for interpreting branching phenotypes. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers accept the mechanistic interpretation without separately evaluating background literature.

OpenEval supports general background claims C105-C110, C115-C116, C120-C128 about neurons, nervous system, and microtubule biology as established scientific knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focus on novel findings rather than general background.

OpenEval supports claims C111-C114, C117-C118 citing prior literature on HMMR's role in development and disease, providing context from ClinVar and published studies. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focus on mechanistic findings in neurons rather than developmental/disease context.

OpenEval rates C119 (human lethality speculation) as UNCERTAIN, noting it's explicitly speculative though reasonable inference from mouse knockout data, appropriately presented as hypothesis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

Peer reviewers support PLA specificity controls (C70, C73) as part of well-controlled experiments demonstrating validity of TPX2-microtubule interaction measurements. OpenEval addresses these controls within R9's broader evaluation of TPX2 findings rather than as a separate result.

Peer reviewers support mechanistic discussion (C92, C94, C104) connecting looped microtubules to branching regulation. OpenEval addresses C92 in R10, C104 in R17 (as UNCERTAIN speculation), and C94 in R10, but peer reviewers treat the overall mechanistic explanation as supported rather than separating speculative elements.
